newsitem.title: UK: Surreal sleaze row hijacks British election.
newsitem.headline: Surreal sleaze row hijacks British election.

text.p: A row over sleaze hijacked the British election campaign on Tuesday when former minister Neil Hamilton confronted an anti-corruption candidate trying to force him to stand down as a candidate for the ruling Conservatives.

The extraordinary row between Hamilton and Martin Bell, a highly respected BBC journalist, came as Bell was about to address an open-air news conference explaining why he was standing in the Tatton constituency of north-west England.
The two, standing inches apart and surrounded by a forest of cameras and microphones, traded verbal thrust and counter-thrust in a surreal stand-off.
Hamilton, who denies allegations that he took cash from a businessman to ask questions in parliament, asked the BBC war correspondent if he was trying to destroy Hamilton's political career.
"The irresistible inference to be drawn from that is that you think I am guilty of corruption in some shape or form," said Hamilton.
Bell, who has dodged bullets for 30 years in wars from Vietnam to Bosnia, answered: "I think the issue of trust is important."
"I have not admitted any mendacity," Hamilton came back.

Hamilton has refused to stand down as Tatton's Conservative candidate in the May 1 election despite being implicated in an influence-peddling scandal that has hurt the ruling party, 20 points behind Labour in national opinion polls.

He faces a final meeting of his local party later on Tuesday when it will decide whether the former trade minister will be their candidate. Some local Conservatives and the opposition Labour and Liberal Democrat parties say he should stand down.
Hamilton's wife Christine asked Bell if he believed her husband was guilty of sleaze. "Do you accept a man is innocent until proved guilty?" she demanded. "Do you then accept my husband is innocent?"
Bell, wearing his trademark white suit worn as a talisman on battlefields around the world, said he would not be drawn into the debate surrounding the cash for questions affair.

"I refuse to be ambushed like this," he said. Bell announced his intention to stand on Sunday. He is supported by both main opposition parties who have withdrawn their candidates. Bell says he will stand down immediately if Hamilton withdraws his candidature.

The media fixation with sleaze, the one constant theme of the first three weeks of campaigning, has deeply angered Prime Minister John Major, who faces an uphill battle to claim a record fifth successive victory for the Conservatives.
The sleaze row also overshadowed a report from Britain's churches that attacked political parties for putting tax cuts for the middle classes before the needs of the poor and jobless.

"In the British general election campaign the political parties are competing for votes by promising low taxation," said the report by the Council of Churches, an umbrella body for Britain and Ireland's main Christian churches.

"When so many are living in poverty and unemployment, it is wrong to give priority to the claims of those who are already well off. None of the political parties has put forward a programme which offers much real hope of improvement to those in greatest need."
